article.title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
article.summary:
But the UK AI minister admitted last week that figure was significantly higher than the government’s actual projections after it was revealed that the assessment came solely from a report commissioned by Google and that its own estimation of AI’s economic benefit was less than a third of that £400 billion figure.
AI minister Kanishka Narayan, answering a parliamentary question on the issue, said that AI adoption and data investment could add £55 billion to £140 billion to the UK economy by 2030, bringing the central estimate to £120 billion.
Narayan said the £400 billion figure “was drawn from a publicly available 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First,” a British consultancy firm now referred to as PF Global.
“AI is a very fast-moving technology, and, as we learn more, we inevitably have to update the assumptions lying behind our models.
The answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it had been wrong.

article.title: Apple's Insider Trading Policy Now Covers Prediction Markets
article.summary:
Apple has added an explicit ban on using confidential information to bet on prediction markets to its insider trading policy, according to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
The new version is marked "Updated October 2026," while an earlier version that Apple filed in 2024 doesn't mention prediction markets at all.
If you haven't heard of them, prediction markets are basically platforms where people buy and sell contracts that pay out depending on whether a future event happens.
Apple also says employees must not share confidential information to others who may go on to use it on such markets.
Apple's insider trading policy applies to directors, officers, employees, independent contractors and consultants, as well as to family members who live with them or are financially dependent on them.

article.title: The polar vortex is about to go haywire

Something “unprecedented” is happening in the atmosphere: the Arctic polar vortex, a spinning mass of air high above the North Pole, is collapsing.
Waves in the atmosphere known as “Rossby waves” can cause the polar vortex to wobble and weaken.
During a big polar vortex disruption—what scientists call a “sudden stratospheric warming”—the vortex can drift, stretch, split into multiple swirls or change direction.
Polar vortex disruptions normally occur deep into the winter, Cohen says, so a sudden stratospheric warming in November is unusual.
“Where everything sets up is still in question.”Not all polar vortex disruptions look the same.

article.title: Why are wealthy countries failing developing nations?
article.summary:
UN report warns climate adaptation funding is falling far short of needsThe United Nations Environment Programme has published a report warning that the world is not adapting quickly enough to keep pace with the growing human and economic costs linked to the climate crisis.
The UN singles out wealthy countries – responsible for the bulk of carbon emissions – for failing to meet their financial pledges.

article.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
article.summary:
Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years.
The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.
Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.
So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.
The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority.

article.title: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
article.summary:
In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government.
